column1: # Where each gloss in lex-ang.tsv was read.
# lemma | pos | tgt | sources | quote | stands
# The gloss is the English word an Old English word is woven for, and the
# tooltip and the word page print it back: it is the claim every reader meets
# first. Every other claim the pack makes about a word names its entry —
# etymons in ang-etymons.tsv, genders in ang-genders.tsv, phrases in
# ang-phrases.tsv — and the gloss named none until 2026-10-07, as the Latin
# The nouns are read so far, all 178 rows; the other parts of speech are the
# next item in TODO.md. On 2026-10-07 every noun was read against English
# Wiktionary's Old English entry, from its raw text, and against
# Bosworth–Toller wherever ang-genders.tsv read the gender there. A script
# drafted a quote for each row from the entry's definition lines, links and
# labels read as the page prints them, and every quote was read against its
# entry; where a page holds more than one word of a spelling — hund, a dog
# and a hundred; lagu, the sea and the law — the quote is from the
# etymology that is this word, as the genders were.
# Each line names the entries it was read in, separated by spaces, the one
#                      (the title drops macrons and the dots of ċ and ġ)
# A noun cites the entry its gender was read in, so the two ledgers cannot
# read different words. Wiktionary files most Old English words under their
# þ spelling, and its page for brōðor, mūð or dēað says only "Alternative
# form of" the þ one; so does its page for meoluc, wall, hæt, wolcen and
# wicu, of meolc, weall, hætt, wolcn and wice. Those twelve lines quote the
# entry named and cite the word's own beside it, and FORM_OF in the test
# lists them. þorp is quoted from Wiktionary, "village", because
# Bosworth–Toller's head, where its gender was read, gives no one English
# word: "the idea at first connected with the words is that of an
# assemblage", then of workers on an estate, and of the estate.
# Blank where the quote holds the row's English word. Otherwise it names the
# word of the quote that stands for it, because the English word is not in the
# entry. Six rows need one: hund for "hound" is "dog", setl for "chair" "seat,
# bench, throne", mentel for "coat" "mantle (kind of cloak)", rīċe for
# "country" "kingdom, empire", fyrhtu for "fear" "fright", and hūsbonda for
# "husband" "master of the house" — the loosest, whose note already says
# One row had no gloss in either dictionary. ċildclāð, woven for "baby"
# until 2026-10-07, is Wiktionary's cildclāþ, "swaddling cloth; (in the
# plural), swaddling clothes", and Bosworth–Toller's "a child-cloth, a
# swaddling-cloth" (bt:6142); its Supplement, where the gender was read, has
# no English at all. Reading this ledger found it, and it was withdrawn the
# same night: "baby" is ċild now, which Wiktionary gives as "child" and
# "baby" and Bosworth–Toller as "a child, infant" (bt:6138). QUEUED in the
# test is for a row like it: one whose line quotes what its entry does say,
# named there until the row is taught differently.
# tests/tools/ang-glosses.test.ts requires every row of a part of speech it
# holds to have a line here, every line to cite Bosworth–Toller or the word's
# own Wiktionary entry, every quote to hold its English word or name the word
# standing for it, no quote to carry wikitext, and every noun to cite the
# entry its gender was read in. It cannot tell a quote somebody copied from
# the entry from one somebody typed, nor an entry somebody read from one
